Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 11093 columns across 1224 data files.

Issues Identified

1014 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 1224 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

We ran the paper’s 1 R script in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • GISD_Generate_Release.R reads B_BeschaeftigteohneAbschluss.xlsx.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

Other problems in the files

  • GISD_Generate_Release.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 1 R code file.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 GISD_Generate_Release.R — none

File paths

2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: Data/Referenz/Referenz_1998_2019.xls to ../Rohdaten/Referenz/Referenz_1998_2019.xls (in GISD_Generate_Release.R); Data/INKAR_1998_2019/ to ../Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/ (in GISD_Generate_Release.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside Rohdaten.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("Rohdaten.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: gem_zipcode_intersections_2015.rdata.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. A script looked for 5 files in another folder than the deposit has them, so before running it once more we copied them there: Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Arbeitslosigkeit.xlsx to Syntax/Data/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Arbeitslosigkeit.xlsx for GISD_Generate_Release.R; Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Beschaeftigtenquote.xlsx to Syntax/Data/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Beschaeftigtenquote.xlsx for GISD_Generate_Release.R; Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Bruttoverdienst.xlsx to Syntax/Data/INKAR_1998_2019/A_Bruttoverdienst.xlsx for GISD_Generate_Release.R; Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/A_ErwerbsfaehigeBevoelkerung.xlsx to Syntax/Data/INKAR_1998_2019/A_ErwerbsfaehigeBevoelkerung.xlsx for GISD_Generate_Release.R; Rohdaten/INKAR_1998_2019/B_BeschaeftigtemitakadAbschluss.xlsx to Syntax/Data/INKAR_1998_2019/B_BeschaeftigtemitakadAbschluss.xlsx for GISD_Generate_Release.R. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
GISD_Generate_Release.R errored runtime 5.2

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

An ethics approval statement was detected, based on the following text:

This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

The Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf has approved this study (study number: 2024-2722).

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
